A beggar is a person who asks strangers or the general public for money, food, or other basic necessities — not as a one-time request to a friend, but as a regular or habitual way of surviving. The crucial idea is that a beggar has little or nothing of their own and depends almost entirely on the generosity of others to get by.

Think of someone sitting on a pavement, holding out a hand or a cup, hoping passersby will drop in some coins. That person is a beggar.
What Makes Someone a Beggar (and What Doesn't)

The defining feature of a beggar is asking for charity from strangers as a means of survival. This separates the word from other related ideas:

  • A poor person is simply someone who lacks money or resources. But a poor person who earns a living — however small — by working, farming, or selling something is not a beggar. The beggar does not (or cannot) earn; they ask.
  • A homeless person may or may not be a beggar. Being without a home and begging are two different things that often — but not always — go together.
  • A thief takes without asking. A beggar asks without taking by force.

So the word sits at a very specific intersection: poor + dependent on others' charity + actively asking.

Beggars typically appear in public places where many people pass — streets, markets, places of worship, bus stops, railway stations. Their "work," so to speak, is making themselves visible and appealing to the sympathy of strangers.

In some parts of the world, begging is also organised — where beggars are managed or exploited by someone else, collecting on behalf of a group or a middleman.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

"Beggar" is a neutral-to-slightly-negative word in modern English. It is not a slur, but it does carry a tone of pity, and historically, some societies have attached shame or low social status to the word. This is why in formal or sensitive writing today, people often prefer phrases like person experiencing homelessness, destitute person, or simply someone begging — to describe the action rather than reduce a person to that one condition.

That said, "beggar" remains perfectly standard and widely used in everyday English. It is not rude in itself.

"Beggars can't be choosers."

This is one of the most well-known English sayings. It means: if you are in a position of need and are depending on others' help, you cannot afford to be fussy or demanding about what you receive. You take what is offered.

For example: Your friend offers you a lift in their old, noisy car. You're stuck and have no other way home. You accept — beggars can't be choosers.

This proverb is used all the time in everyday conversation, well beyond the literal context of actual beggars.

"A beggar on horseback" (or: "Set a beggar on horseback and he'll ride to the devil.")

This is an older proverb meaning: when a person who has always been poor or of low status suddenly gets power, wealth, or authority, they often become arrogant, reckless, or corrupt — even worse than someone who was always privileged and knew how to handle it.

In British English, "beggar" is also used as a light, informal term for a person — often with affection, sympathy, or mild envy, not related to poverty at all.

  • "You lucky beggar!" — said to a friend who just won something.
  • "Poor beggar" — said sympathetically about someone going through a hard time.
  • "Cheeky beggar!" — said about someone being audaciously bold or shameless.

In this use, the word has completely shed its literal meaning. It functions almost like calling someone a rascal or fellow. This is informal and largely British — you would not typically hear this in American English.

In some traditions, begging is not a sign of shame but of spiritual humility. Buddhist monks in South and Southeast Asia, for example, walk in the morning with their bowls and accept food from laypeople — this is a sacred act on both sides. The monk begs as a form of renunciation (giving up worldly ownership), and the giver earns merit. Similarly, medieval Christian friars (called mendicants, from a formal Latin-rooted word meaning "beggars") lived by begging as a deliberate religious choice.

So while in everyday life being a beggar implies hardship, in spiritual contexts it can mean voluntary poverty and dependence on community.

A beggar is a person who survives by asking others — usually strangers — for money or basic necessities, having no sufficient means of their own; the word also appears in fixed expressions like "beggars can't be choosers" and, in informal British use, as a mild affectionate term for any person.
